Role Summary
About the role
The British Museum is seeking a Project Curator to join the department of Africa, Oceania and the Americas.  Working on the
African Histories and Heritage Programme
, you will play a leading role in the delivery of the project: ‘Reconnecting Eastern African Collections and Histories’ (REACH).
REACH is a new 4-year research and education project aiming to significantly expand knowledge of the British Museum’s Eastern Africa collection and increase its impact. This project will produce an object-based history of the ivory caravan trade and imposition of colonial rule (c1800-1914) in Eastern Africa. Working in collaboration with an international network of partner museums and community stakeholders in Tanzania, Kenya and Uganda, the team will generate new knowledge about museum collections, build strong relationships between partners and share knowledge in East Africa through bespoke schools’ programmes and other activities.
You will play a vital role in connecting people with the collection, expanding curatorial practice and advancing interpretations of African histories and heritage at the British Museum.

Job Description
Applications are once again open to join Co-operatives UK's Youth Advisory Group (YAG) - young people aged 16-30 are invited to apply.
Established in 2024, the   YAG brings together 16-30-year-olds from across the co-operative landscape to provide strategic input into Co-operatives UK's work - and to collaborate on independent projects aimed at increasing engagement among young people across the movement and society in general.
It was launched at Co-operatives UK's National Youth Summit in 2024 to support the organisation in implementing one of its strategy's core themes: empowering young people.
Advise and enrich
Young people bring new perspectives to our work; provide valuable insight; generate new ideas; and challenge our way of thinking. The Youth Advisory Group will shape what we do to ensure it aligns with the needs of young people. Members of the Group will work alongside us to champion youth voice and advocate for meaningful participation within the co-operative movement.
Advocate and engage
Young people today are facing an uncertain future, where climate anxiety and job insecurity are major factors in their lives. While we know that the co-operative movement offers solutions to enable a fairer future, many young people are unaware. A key role of the Youth Advisory Group will be to advocate for the movement, spreading the word about co-ops and promoting the values of co-operation within youth networks outside the movement.

Recent breakthroughs in stem cell biology, organoid culture and bioengineering provide unprecedented opportunities to recreate complex aspects of human biology in a dish. However, current three-dimensional culture systems often lack the spatial organisation, cellular complexity and tissue architecture required to faithfully recapitulate human physiology. Here, we aim to harness next-generation bioprinting to develop clinically relevant New Alternative Methodologies (NAMs) for modelling human biology in vitro.
The Boroviak Lab are looking for a highly motivated Research Assistant to support our bioprinting efforts at the Cambridge Stem Cell Institute. The project aims to combine stem cell biology, tissue culture and bioengineering with state-of-the-art bioprinting to generate physiologically relevant three-dimensional models of human tissues. The successful candidate will work closely with members of the Boroviak Lab and our collaborators across the Stem Cell Institute to establish and characterise new bioprinted tissue models.
This is an exciting opportunity to work at the interface of stem cell biology and bioengineering, with the opportunity to develop new approaches to study human disease in vitro.
The postholder will actively contribute to our research and be responsible for the establishment, optimisation and characterisation of bioprinted tissue models. The candidate will have an excellent background in biology and previous laboratory experience. Experience with mammalian tissue culture and particularly stem cell or organoid culture would be ideal. Previous experience in bioengineering, biomaterials, three-dimensional culture or bioprinting would be advantageous, but is not essential. Most importantly, we are looking for a highly motivated, curious and collaborative individual who is keen to learn new approaches and develop innovative experimental strategies. https://www.cam.ac.uk/jobs/research-assi.title: Research Assistant/associate in development of 4D image processing methods (Fixed Term)
https://www.cam.ac.uk/jobs/research-assi.description:
The post holder will be located in Central Cambridge, UK.
Computed tomography (CT) has transformed fields by enabling non-destructive three-dimensional (3D) imaging. However, conventional CT is fundamentally limited by acquisition speed: high-quality 3D reconstruction typically requires thousands of X-ray radiographs acquired over a full specimen rotation, taking minutes to hours. This makes CT unsuitable for fast, transient phenomena such as additive manufacturing, impact, fracture and high-rate deformation.
We are launching an ambitious research programme to overcome this limitation and establish new approaches for X-ray tomography of rapidly evolving processes. Combining advances in X-ray hardware, computational imaging, machine learning and mechanics, the project aims to reconstruct the three-dimensional evolution of materials during dynamic deformation, moving beyond static CT towards true four-dimensional imaging in space and time.
We seek an outstanding Research Associate/Research Assistant to play a leading role in developing the computational foundations of this programme. The successful candidate will develop reconstruction and image-processing methods for highly under sampled, dynamically evolving X-ray datasets, including approaches based on neural radiance fields (NeRFs), neural representations and related state-of-the-art computational imaging techniques.
A central challenge will be to combine X-ray measurements with physical knowledge of deformation processes. The project therefore offers significant scope to develop new physics-informed and data-driven approaches coupling computational imaging with models of material deformation, with considerable freedom to shape the computational research programme.

https://www.cam.ac.uk/jobs/research-asso.description:
Oligodendrocyte progenitor cells are now recognised as stem cells of the adult brain, recruited for learning and repair throughout life. This project aims at testing innovative ways of recruiting oligodendrocyte lineage cells in neurodegenerative disease by targeting metabolic pathways.
This post is part of a new collaborative research programme at the University of Cambridge based across the laboratories of Professor Clémence Blouet (Institute of Metabolic Science) and Professor Ragnhildur Thóra Káradóttir (Cambridge Stem Cell Institute; Director of the MS Society Cambridge Centre for Myelin Repair). The project is funded by Eli Lilly and will test the idea that targeting incretin receptor agonists can promote remyelination and support brain repair in progressive multiple sclerosis.
The successful candidate will work across both laboratories. The project will involve focal demyelinating lesion models, stereotaxic surgery and pharmacological interventions, in vivo recordings of neuronal activity, histology and imaging, and single-nucleus transcriptomics.
This is a unique opportunity to work at the interface of metabolic science and neuroscience in a collaborative translational environment, with access to state-of-the-art facilities across the Cambridge Stem Cell Institute, the Institute of Metabolic Science, and the wider Cambridge Biomedical Campus.
Requirements:
Applicants should hold a PhD in neuroscience or a related discipline. A strong background in in vivo rodent work is essential. Experience with several of the required techniques is important, including stereotaxic surgery, histology, imaging, or electrophysiological techniques, particularly in vivo. We will provide training where needed . The successful candidate must be highly organised, able to work both independently and collaboratively, and have strong analytical and communication skills.

A Research Associate post is available in the Marine Ecology and Conservation Group, led by Dr Catharine Horswill, in the Department of Zoology at the University of Cambridge. Catharine is a quantitative marine ecologist with expertise in population modelling, demography and the application of ecological evidence to conservation and management.
Reliable stock assessments are essential for the sustainable management of tropical tuna fisheries worldwide. In representing complex population and fishery dynamics, assessment models rely on simplifying assumptions about biological processes, spatial structure and fisheries data. Understanding how these assumptions affect model performance and management advice is critical for identifying key sources of uncertainty and determining where methodological advances or improvements in fisheries data could most effectively strengthen future assessments.
The project will develop and apply high-resolution, simulation-based approaches to evaluate how assumptions about population biology and fisheries data influence stock assessment performance and management advice. The project will initially focus on Indian Ocean yellowfin tuna, with subsequent application to bigeye and skipjack tuna where appropriate.
Initial work will build on an existing high-resolution, spatially explicit simulation framework developed using the Spatial Population Model (SPM). SPM will be used to generate population and fishery scenarios that incorporate key sources of structural uncertainty, including spatial variation in growth and fishery selectivity, alternative population structures, and differences in the weighting of fisheries data. Assessment models, including Stock Synthesis (SS3) and next-generation platforms such as SPoRC (
https://chengmatt.github.io/SPoRC/

Led by Jacksons Lane in partnership with Bruce Castle Museum & Archive, the 'Acts of Change: Young People & the Nicky Gavron Archive' is an Archives Revealed funded project. The project will preserve, catalogue and activate the personal archive of Nicky Gavron, a founding community leader of Jacksons Lane and pivotal figure in Haringey's civic, environmental and cultural history. Bruce Castle are the owners and permanent keepers of the archive, ensuring long   term care and public stewardship.
The archive comprises around 70 unsorted boxes spanning 1970s-2010s documenting the development of Jacksons Lane alongside movements in community arts, disability arts, local government activism and cultural policy. Materials include correspondence, campaign papers, drawings, photographs, minutes, fundraising records and press. Its scale and lack of order prevent public access and pose risks to long   term preservation.
Over nine months, the Project Archivist will catalogue the collection to recognised standards, assisted by MA Archive Management and History placements and supervised by the Archivist at Bruce Castle Museum & Archive. A key public outcome will be a freely accessible online catalogue, enabling public discovery for the first time.
The Project Archivist will also support the engagement team to deliver a youth-led programme inspired by Gavron's commitment to young people. Twelve Young Heritage Producers aged 16-21 will explore the archive and co-create public outcomes, including workshops, a public event at Bruce Castle with selected elements shared at Jacksons Lane, and a digital legacy output such as a zine or exhibition guide.

https://biffilab.wordpress.com
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains a formidable clinical challenge. A major recent advance has been the development of KRAS inhibitors, which have shown considerable promise in clinical trials (1). For decades, KRAS was considered undruggable; however, these new inhibitors represent a potential turning point for patients with PDAC. Despite this progress, rapid therapy resistance has already been observed in both patients and pre-clinical mouse models, highlighting the urgent need to define the mechanisms that drive resistance and to identify rational combination therapies.
In our laboratory, we have established and validated a panel of genetically heterogeneous PDAC models. These studies have shown that malignant-cell genetics shape distinct, therapeutically actionable vulnerabilities through both cell-intrinsic programmes and changes in the surrounding tumour microenvironment [(2) and unpublished]. These observations create an important opportunity: we hypothesise that malignant¿stromal crosstalk within defined genetic contexts drives distinct mechanisms of resistance to KRAS inhibition. In support of this, our work indicates that cancer-associated fibroblasts play diverse roles in PDAC progression and activate pathways that may contribute to therapy resistance (3, 4). This PhD project will therefore identify malignant cell-intrinsic and malignant cell-extrinsic mechanisms of resistance to KRAS inhibition, including fibroblast-mediated mechanisms, across genetically distinct PDACs. We will prioritise PDAC genotypes for which we already have preliminary data suggesting candidate mechanisms of resistance.

A research assistant position has become available to aid the running of the busy, expanding shared laboratory resource in the Cambridge Biomedical Research Centre Cell Phenotyping Hub. The role will be covering all three Hub sites located at Addenbrooke's Hospital, Jeffrey Cheah Biomedical Centre and Victor Dahdaleh Heart and Lung Research Institute.  The BRC Cell Phenotyping Hub is a science technology platform providing services in cytomics in the Clinical School and across Cambridge Biomedical Campus. It is equipped with state-of-the-art-specialist cytomics equipment including multiple sorters and analysers, magnetic separator, two confocal and an epifluorescence microscope, laser capture microscope, high content array scan and other kits.
We are looking for a highly motivated and proactive individual to support multiple laboratory routine techniques.  Daily tasks will include flow sorting, magnetic cell separation, cell processing, phenotyping and at a later stage other molecular and cell biology techniques. It is a fully integrated Hub role with varied research and service responsibilities. The role holder will be supporting different teams working on various research projects, thereby making a significant contribution to translational biomedical research at University of Cambridge. The role holder may be providing some focused support to a research fellow, analyst and/or group leader in the Phenotyping Hub. In addition, the role holder will undertake tasks of supporting the operations through general laboratory, administrative, record keeping and maintenance duties as well as through a contribution to training and teaching.
The successful candidate should have hands-on experience in cytometry, cell separation (FACS and MACS, imaging, high content/ throughput analysis) and ideally some expertise in tissue culture and cell, immunological and molecular methods. Sorting experience is a distinct advantage but full training will be  given to a successful candidate.

The Ali Lab wishes to recruit a student to work on the project entitled: "Discovery of rational therapeutic biomarkers in breast cancer by systems pathology and deep learning".

Project details
The therapeutic landscape for breast cancer patients is rapidly evolving with novel therapies regularly receiving regulatory approval. Yet directing these treatments to patients likely to benefit while sparing those unlikely to respond from their toxicities remains a major challenge. Many modern therapies, like immunotherapy and ADCs, rely on tissue architecture to be effective. Intercellular relationships in breast cancer tissues also determine cellular activation states and expression profiles, rendering some cells susceptible and others resistant to new treatments.
The aim of this project is to use modern multiomic spatial methods (in which our group has extensive expertise1¿4) together with deep learning (for efficient representation and cross-modal learning) to discover the potential therapeutic landscape for novel therapies in breast cancer, and to propose rational multidimensional biomarkers for combinatorial therapy. We are generating multimodal spatial datasets in cohorts of breast cancer patients (the largest of their kind; making extensive use of imaging mass cytometry and spatial transcriptomics) that span observational studies and clinical trials. We must precisely define the landscape of novel target expression, quantify its heterogeneity, and the contribution of tissue architecture as a determinant of expression profiles. For further information about the research group, including their most recent publications, please visit their website at

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains a formidable clinical challenge. A major recent advance has been the development of KRAS inhibitors, which have shown considerable promise in clinical trials (1). For decades, KRAS was considered undruggable; however, these new inhibitors represent a potential turning point for patients with PDAC. Despite this progress, rapid therapy resistance has already been observed in both patients and pre-clinical mouse models, highlighting the urgent need to define the mechanisms that drive resistance and to identify rational combination therapies.
In our laboratory, we have established and validated a panel of genetically heterogeneous PDAC models. These studies have shown that malignant-cell genetics shape distinct, therapeutically actionable vulnerabilities through both cell-intrinsic programmes and changes in the surrounding tumour microenvironment [(2) and unpublished]. These observations create an important opportunity: we hypothesise that malignant¿stromal crosstalk within defined genetic contexts drives distinct mechanisms of resistance to KRAS inhibition. In support of this, our work indicates that cancer-associated fibroblasts play diverse roles in PDAC progression and activate pathways that may contribute to therapy resistance (3, 4). This PhD project will therefore identify malignant cell-intrinsic and malignant cell-extrinsic mechanisms of resistance to KRAS inhibition, including fibroblast-mediated mechanisms, across genetically distinct PDACs. We will prioritise PDAC genotypes for which we already have preliminary data suggesting candidate mechanisms of resistance.

Collections Care Assistant (21 hours, FTC to March 2028)
Looking to build your collections care career in the world's first railway town?
About the role
Locomotion in Shildon sits in the world's first railway town, on the site where the first steam-hauled passenger train left for Stockton in 1825. Today we care for the national collection of rail vehicles here, alongside a group of Grade II listed buildings that includes Soho Shed. Since New Hall opened in 2024, close to 100 vehicles have been on display - the largest undercover collection of historic rail vehicles in Europe - and the bicentenary has brought record numbers of visitors through the site.
We are looking for a Collections Care Assistant to join our Collections Care team during this busy and exciting time. You will be involved in a wide variety of conservation and collections care activities, including environmental monitoring, integrated pest management and conservation cleaning, as well as condition reporting, data management and recording. This role offers performance development and training opportunities.
This is a part-time role of 21 hours per week, offered on a fixed term contract to March 2028. The salary is £24,479 full time equivalent, which is £14,687 pro rated for 21 hours. We're flexible about how those hours are worked across the week and will agree a pattern with you when you join. In the early months we'd expect your days to line up with our Senior Conservator's, so you get the training and support you need on site, and once you're settled there's real scope to shape the pattern around what works for you.

The conventional account of fundamental physics begins with a Lagrangian, derives its observable consequences and ends with a comparison against data. In modern cosmology, the middle of this process has become the difficult part. New theories require substantial calculations, specialised numerical methods and research software capable of carrying their predictions through to cosmological observables. Much of this machinery is concentrated in large collaborations and established frameworks, while tractability at cosmological scales often relies on effective descriptions which have integrated out the physics under investigation.
This creates a bias in which theories are tested. So long as it is substantially harder to investigate a new theory from scratch than to rerun an established model, our attention will be directed towards the theories which are easiest to implement rather than those which are most scientifically promising.

As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly prominent in this field, its adoption into clinical practice depends on rigorous evidence from both retrospective and prospective studies.
Our group is working on a suite of research within breast cancer screening and we're seeking a highly motivated individual with a broad skillset for this role as a key team member in driving projects forwards. The role will span from curating dataset for use in retrospective evaluation of AI tools to supporting large, prospective clinical trials in which these tools are being deployed.

It is currently being used to evaluate commercial AI tools for cancer detection and for predicting cancers that may develop within 3¿5 years following a negative mammogram. This role provides scope not only to support these evaluations but also to develop and test your own models.
The role will also see the expansion of CC-MEDIA, collecting and curating screening data from sites using mammography equipment from different vendors. This is for use in a vital step of the EDITH trial (Early Detection using Information technology in Health) where we are responsible for benchmarking algorithms hoping to enter the study. The EDITH trial will recruit 660,000 women from screening centres across the UK and their mammograms will be collected by the Cambridge site to facilitate comparison testing of AI tools at the end of recruitment. A successful candidate will be comfortable working with large medical datasets and data processing pipelines.

Preservation Technician
What It's Like to Work Here
At IWM, we're driven by a shared purpose: helping people understand the impact of conflict and the experiences of those affected by it. Our collections are among the most significant of their kind and play a vital role in preserving and sharing these stories with audiences today and in the future. You'll join a collaborative team of specialists who are passionate about collections care, preservation excellence and making history accessible through exhibitions, research and public engagement.
Why This Role Matters
The Preservation Technician plays an important role in protecting and caring for IWM's collections across multiple sites. Through preventive conservation activities, environmental monitoring and collections care, you'll help ensure that historic objects remain safe, accessible and suitable for display, storage, research and learning.
Your work will directly support exhibitions, filming projects, loans, storage initiatives and public access programmes. By helping prevent deterioration, managing risks and maintaining high preservation standards, you'll contribute to safeguarding nationally significant collections for future generations.

Deliver conservation cleaning and preventive conservation activities for collections on display and in storage.
Monitor environmental conditions, support Integrated Pest Management programmes and identify preservation risks.
Handle, pack, move and care for collection objects safely and in line with professional standards.

About Us
The Faculty of Life Sciences & Medicine is one of the largest and most successful centres for research and education in the UK. The Faculty was created as a result of the merger of elements of the School of Biomedical Sciences with the School of Medicine. The merger brings together basic, translational and clinical scientists to provide new cross-School research collaborations while optimising the deployment of teaching expertise across the Faculty. The Faculty has unparalleled expertise in basic, translational and clinical research; analytical and forensic science; asthma and allergy; biophysics and cell biology;
cancer; cardiovascular; nutrition and diabetes; genetics; infection and immunology; imaging and biomedical engineering; transplantation immunology; pharmaceutical science; physiology and women's health. We also have thriving research programmes in global health, and health and social care.
Within FoLSM, the School of Biomedical Engineering and Imaging Sciences is a cutting-edge research and teaching School dedicated to development, translation and clinical application within medical imaging and computational modelling technologies. Our objective is to facilitate research and teaching guided by clinical questions and is aimed at novelty, understanding of physiology and pathophysiology as well as development of new diagnostic tools and therapies. In this way, basic science can be rapidly translated into clinical applications (and vice versa). The project will build on established and newly generated datasets to understand how tumour metabolism varies between and within patients, how metabolic state shapes tumour phenotype and heterogeneity, and how these processes influence response to therapy.

Please note this is a single role, however the role-holder will hold two 50% contracts in parallel to reflect the key responsibilities of the role (Research and Academic-related).
The Mapping Archaeological Heritage in South Asia (MAHSA) project, funded by Arcadia, aims to protect endangered archaeological and cultural heritage across the Indus River Basin in Pakistan and northwest India. These regions are rich in historical sites, yet face growing threats from development, agriculture, and erosion. MAHSA uses satellite imagery, historical mapping, machine learning, published data and new on-the-ground discoveries to identify and assess at-risk sites, transform legacy data, and fill gaps in spatial coverage.
The Exhibition, Between the Lines: Mapping Histories in the Margins, is scheduled to open in 2029. It will tell the story of South Asian people and places whose histories have been lost and found, forgotten and remembered and explore how digital technologies can foster new stories, connections, and interactions, showcasing collections drawn from across the University of Cambridge Museums (UCM). 
The Museum of Archaeology and Anthropology (MAA) is one of the nine University of Cambridge Museums and Botanic Garden (UCM). It a key resource for University teaching and research. Its world-class collections attract visiting researchers from all over the world and it maintains an active programme of temporary exhibitions and loans to major exhibitions within the UK and internationally. MAA's collections are Designated for their national and international importance.

The Museum of Archaeology and Anthropology is seeking to appoint Archivist (0.4FTE).
The Museum of Archaeology and Anthropology holds world-class collections of anthropology and archaeology. The Museum's collections are formally Designated by DCMS in their entirety and are made up of four main bodies of material: archaeological and anthropological artefacts, including many outstanding works of world art, photographs, and an archive. The archive is a rich resource, estimated to be over 50,000 documents, embracing an extraordinary range of travellers' and scientists' letters, primary field journals, notes and drawings, records of Museum acquisitions and of Museum history. The documents are important to research fields from art and archaeology, Indigenous cultures, artefact provenances, to the formation of archaeology and anthropology in Britain, and the activities of many famous scientists.
The main purpose of this role is to make the material accessible to researchers and staff. The Archivist will include appraising documents, working to arrange and describe material, create digital records, and rehouse materials, flagging any issues that require conservation. They will work with the support of a working group, of MAA staff and senior external archivists, to guide and support the activity.
The successful candidate will have relevant experience of working with archive material in a relevant setting. They will have experience in using an automated library or archives management system and supervising the work of a small team of volunteers. Working knowledge of archival cataloguing standards, including ISAD(G) and EAD are essential to the role, as are good attention to detail and the ability to work independently and as part of a team. They will be hold a postgraduate qualification in archives or record management, or have relevant comparable experience.

We invite applications for a 2-year Postdoctoral Research Associate position in Nucleic Acid Computing and Molecular Programming in the laboratory of Dr Gamze Gursoy at the University of Cambridge.
The successful candidate will join an interdisciplinary research programme at the interface of biochemistry, molecular biology, biomolecular engineering, and computational genomics. The current focus is developing new technologies for genetic privacy, a problem requiring molecular and computational systems to be designed together rather than sequentially.
The postholder will join an active team developing programmable nucleic-acid systems that sense defined human genomic sequences and convert those molecular recognition events into engineered DNA outputs. The broader aim is to develop molecular systems in which useful genetic information can be measured while limiting direct exposure of the underlying genomic sequence. The successful candidate will help design, build, validate, and iteratively improve these systems, and extend them toward robust, multiplexed privacy-preserving applications.
This is primarily an experimental, bench-based position. We are looking for a researcher who enjoys designing and building molecular systems rather than applying established protocols. The postholder will also engage directly with quantitative data generated by their experiments: analysing assay performance, identifying failure modes, comparing alternative designs, and using those results to determine the next experimental iteration. Extensive computational genomics experience is not required, but the ability and willingness to work quantitatively with one's own experimental data is important.
The appointee will be expected to plan and manage their own research and administration, with guidance from the PI as required. They will take an active role in the research group, contribute to graduate student research skills, and participate in seminars, workshops, and interdisciplinary collab

One topic where Cambridge has a long history is black holes, the most extreme environments in nature, and laboratories where strong gravity, plasma physics and high-energy astro(particle)/physical processes meet. The research group of Prof. Sera Markoff (Plumian Professor) studies these systems across the full black hole mass scale, combining GPU-accelerated supercomputer simulations and semi-analytic modelling with data from world-leading facilities including the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT). About us:
The Centre for Neuroimaging Sciences (CNS) at the Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology & Neuroscience (IoPPN), King’s College London, is a world-leading research centre specialising in neuroimaging and psychopharmacology. Our multidisciplinary teams combine expertise in neuroscience, psychiatry, imaging, and pharmacology to explore how drugs and psychiatric conditions influence brain function and behaviour. With state-of-the-art MRI, PET, and EEG facilities, the CNS provides a dynamic environment for investigating the neurobiological mechanisms underlying mental health and the effects of novel pharmacological compounds. This role offers the opportunity to contribute to cutting-edge translational research within one of the UK’s leading research centres.
About the role:
This is a full-time post and you will be offered a fixed term contract until 31st August 2029.
Applications are invited for a Clinical Research Fellow to lead cutting-edge translational research within the Department of Neuroimaging. The post-holder will be responsible for running a patient-facing neuroimaging study investigating paranoia in individuals with a diagnosis of psychosis, collecting a range of clinical, imaging, behavioural, and cognitive data.
Additionally, the candidate will act as the clinical lead for two experimental psychopharmacology studies examining paranoia in healthy volunteers following the administration of THC, the main active component of cannabis.

Fixed-term: The funds for this post are available for 18 months in the first instance, if project milestone targets are met at 18 months, a further 18 months of funding will be allocated.
Applications are invited for a Postdoctoral Research Associate (PDRA) to develop custom optics integrated with microfluidic ultra-high-throughput screening (uHTS) for label free screening of phase separation in de novo designed inorganic-protein hybrid materials. Techniques developed include polarised optical microscopy (POM), fluorescence microscopy, and darkfield microscopy, coupled to droplet microfluidics for screening for libraries of 10K to >1M samples. Scientific objectives are to map the phase space of ordered inorganic hybrid materials. Screens will explore the multidimensional parameter sampling of reaction conditions and libraries of de novo inorganic-templating interfaces. The PDRA will be hosted in the group of Professor Knowles in the Department of Chemistry at Cambridge University, funded by an Advanced Research + Invention Agency (ARIA) international consortium.
The PDRA will be responsible for designing, assembling, and maintaining microscopes which integrate polarisation-resolved and fluorescence optics with existing custom microfluidic droplet screening platforms including PhaseScan and cell free expression.
Training in microfluidics will be provided. The Knowles group brings expertise in droplet-based screening, soft matter physics, biophysics, and phase separation, and the post holder is not expected to arrive with that background. Consortium partners bring expertise in de novo protein design and high-throughput inorganic synthesis. Collaborating closely with these partners, the PDRA will design, build, and utilise systems to enable uHTS to be extended to de novo designed inorganic-protein composites, identifying and optimising conditions which produce functional hybrid materials.

A Research Associate post is available in the Behaviour and Evolution Group directed by Rufus Johnstone in the Department of Zoology at the University of Cambridge.
The applicant will join an exciting, inter-disciplinary team investigating the role of intergroup conflict in the evolution of animal societies. Informed by data collected from banded mongoose and termite study systems, the applicant will develop new theoretical models of intergroup conflict, as part of an ERC Advanced Grant (INTERGROUP) awarded to Rufus Johnstone and Michael Cant and funded by the UKRI under the Horizon Guarantee programme.
Intergroup conflict is recognised as a potentially powerful force shaping the evolution of social behaviour in animal societies. However, we have limited theory to explain and predict when intergroup fights will break out, how long they will last, how they end, or their consequences for individual behaviour and life history. This successful applicant will address these questions by developing new theoretical models of conflict initiation,
dynamics, and consequences for life history allocation. The goal of the modelling work is to generate predictions that can be tested using data from the mongoose and termite systems or published data in other taxa.
The successful applicant will join the Behaviour and Evolution research group based in the Department of Zoology, directed by Rufus Johnstone. They will form part of the larger group of researchers working on the INTERGROUP project based at the universities of Exeter, Swansea, Liverpool John Moores and York. They will participate in regular meetings with the team, with potential opportunities for collaboration and short visits as the project develops. Candidates will be highly motivated and keen to interact with other components of the wider project. The Aviation Impact Accelerator (AIA) at the University of Cambridge seeks to recruit Technical Analyst who will be based at the Whittle Laboratory in West Cambridge. The research carried out by the AIA is critically dependent upon robust modelling and analysis to support its mission of transforming aviation toward a net-zero future. This role has been created to align with the design and delivery of innovative tools and services that underpin cutting-edge research in sustainable aviation.
To assist the AIA in achieving its objectives, you will develop and operate models that assess the economic and environmental outcomes of aviation systems. You will also contribute to external reports and grant proposals under the supervision of the line manager, while engaging with stakeholders across academia, industry, and policy domains to ensure impactful delivery of research outputs.
The Aviation Impact Accelerator (AIA) uses a combination of physics-based and data-driven modelling to develop its first-order models of the aviation sector and beyond. These models compose to create a single comprehensive systems-of-systems model. In contrast to most academic modelling, we lean heavily on functional programming as a paradigm as this, along with computer algebra, immutability, and more, allows the computational implementations of our models to align more closely with their mathematics. The AIA's modelling toolboxes (there is broadly one per aviation system being modelled) are written in modern typed Python. About 90% of our current software development is greenfield, meaning that everyone helps shape the architecture of, and idioms used in, our codebases.
You will have an undergraduate degree in STEM (engineering, mathematics, physics, environmental sciences, or a related field), or equivalent practical experience. You will possess strong software skills preferably in Python, alongside proficiency in modelling and data analysis. Excellent verbal and written communication skills

The Community Brain, in partnership with South West London and St George’s Mental Health NHS Trust, is inviting artists and creative practitioners to become part of a creative programme for the new Tolworth Hospital. This brief is for the Storytelling & Co-design, ‘The Narrator’ opportunity.

Alongside the individual artwork commissions, we want to create an opportunity to capture and creatively interpret the story of the programme as it develops.
We are therefore looking for an artist, collective or creative team to act as 'The Narrator' for Art for Tolworth.
The Narrator will work across the programme, developing relationships with the people involved and finding creative ways to gather, interpret and make visible the conversations, ideas, experiences, processes and making that emerge.
We are not looking simply for conventional project documentation. We want the process of observing, gathering, recording and interpreting Art for Tolworth to become creative work in its own right.
The final form is deliberately open. It might involve visual art, drawing, writing, photography, film, sound, illustration, publishing, objects, installation, digital work, participatory practice, archives, collected material or combinations of different approaches.

Claude Blair (1922-2010) was an internationally renowned expert on European arms and armour, publishing extensively on the topic. He began his museum career at the Tower of London and later moved to the Victoria and Albert Museum, where he became Keeper of Metalwork. His archive at the Wallace Collection consists of correspondences, notes, photographs and personal papers, related to his research, publications, extensive career and role as a founding member of the Church Monuments Society.
The Project Cataloguer will be responsible for cataloguing the remainder of the Blair Archive, which has already been box-listed, with cataloguing work currently underway. This is an exciting opportunity to work with a diverse and fascinating collection, including material relating to arms and armour and medieval history.
The position will sit within the Curatorial team, reporting to the Archivist.

https://www.cam.ac.uk/jobs/research-asso.description:
How do mutant clones compete in healthy tissues as animals age, and how do some mammals suppress cancer across remarkably different lifespans and body sizes? The Cagan Lab is recruiting a Postdoctoral Research Associate to investigate these questions through comparative somatic genomics.
The Cagan Lab uses natural variation across species as a powerful experiment. Mammals differ dramatically in lifespan, body size, life history and cancer incidence. Comparing them can reveal the general rules of clonal evolution, expose lineage-specific solutions to cancer suppression, and provide a principled way to interpret emerging findings from human tissues.
This pioneering project will map age-related clonal dynamics across mammals with diverse lifespans and body-sizes including rodents, elephants and cetaceans. The aim is to uncover principles governing somatic evolution in mammals. Comparing somatic and germline tissues will reveal how clones arise and expand, which genes and pathways are selected, and how tissue context and species biology influence these processes.
The role is predominantly computational, with an experimental data-generation component and substantial intellectual ownership. You will combine high-depth error-corrected sequencing (NanoSeq), species-specific targeted gene panels, histology and quantitative evolutionary analysis. The balance of computational and experimental work will vary as the project develops.
Key responsibilities
Develop reproducible genomic workflows; call and quality-control somatic variants; quantify mutation rates and signatures; infer clone sizes and dynamics; and test for selection.
Design targeted gene panels and comparative analyses accounting for species, tissue, age, sex and sampling structure. Model clonal growth in relation to lifespan, body size, tissue architecture and cancer risk, including comparisons with human datasets.

Experience in next generation sequencing and/or bioinformatics will be advantageous. With recent long-term funding awarded, you will be joining the group at a formative time. You will be enthusiastic about being part of a growing group. This position is a staff vacancy at the University of Cambridge that would allow for the post holder to also undertake a postgraduate course at the University, should an offer of a place be made following the relevant competitive process.

The Research
Luke Harland is establishing a new research group based in the Loke Centre for Trophoblast Research within the Department of Physiology, Development and Neuroscience at the University of Cambridge. The group investigates how specialised blood and vascular cell types arise during mammalian development and uses this knowledge to generate defined cell populations from pluripotent stem cells for mechanistic studies and tissue modelling.
We aim to understand how developmental history shapes blood and vascular cell identity and function, and to apply this knowledge to build improved vascularised tissue models. By recreating the developmental processes that generate specialised blood vessels, we hope to build more physiologically relevant models for studying human development and disease. Our initial focus is on reconstructing the fetal placental exchange interface, which enables the transfer of oxygen and nutrients required for fetal growth and development.
Our research combines embryology, stem cell biology, single-cell genomics, genome engineering, advanced imaging and computational biology.
Further information about Luke Harland and key publications relevant to the ongoing research programme can be found on the Loke Centre for Trophoblast Research website (
https://www.trophoblast.cam.ac.uk/people/luke-harland
)
The Opportunity
We are seeking an enthusiastic and motivated Research Assistant to join our growing Wellcome-funded research programme. This is an exciting opportunity to become one of the founding members of a new research group and contribute to its development and culture.
The successful candidate will contribute to research spanning developmental and stem cell biology, with opportunities to work with pluripotent stem cell culture and directed differentiation, molecular biology, flow cytometry, microscopy, mouse developmental models and single-cell genomics.

The University Counselling and Wellbeing Service (Student Support) is a dynamic, high-demand service driven by our mission to support and empower students in fulfilling their academic and personal potential.
We are at an exciting stage of the service's development. Following a transformative Student Mental Health and Wellbeing Plan (2022-2025) at the Collegiate University, we are recruiting to a number of roles to support our service's work and objectives under a new Student Support strategic plan (2026-2029). As part of an integrated Student Support Department, we work in partnership with the Mental Health Advice Service, the Harassment and Violence Support Service, and the Accessibility and Disability Resource to offer students joined-up support. These services contribute to a wider stepped care approach at Collegiate Cambridge, working in partnership with College Health and Wellbeing teams who support students in their College community.
We are seeking to appoint a highly-motivated, experienced professional in the field of counselling and psychotherapy to the new role of Senior Counsellor (Access and Wellbeing). The Senior Counsellor (Access and Wellbeing) plays a crucial operational role within a high-demand student support service, supporting the diverse needs of Cambridge's student population. We are keen to build a cast that reflects the rich diversity of modern British families and communities, bringing a range of lived experiences and backgrounds to the world of the play.

Applications are invited for a postdoctoral position to start from January 2027 or as soon as possible after this date. This project is funded by a grant from the ERC and aims to elucidate mechanisms of antibacterial and antiviral immunity in birds.
The main focus of the research will be to characterise the innate immune complexes which form in avian cells in response to infection and to discover how they resemble or differ from human systems. Recent advances have found a critical role for protein concentration in the formation of such molecular assemblies which requires investigation of genes using precise gene editing. Isolation of signalling complexes will be followed by proteomic analysis of their contents in a time- and stimulus-dependent manner.
Applicants should have a PhD in cell biology, evolutionary biology, immunology or a related discipline. Essential wet lab skills will be experience with cell culture, CRISPR-based gene editing and in vitro infection studies. A good understanding of human and avian innate immunity and evolutionary bioinformatics would be an advantage. The project is in collaboration with other postdocs within and outside the department. The candidate must value teamwork and collaboration, and have good administrative, interpersonal and presentational skills.
We are committed to a proactive approach to equality, which includes supporting and encouraging equally all groups of individuals, promoting an inclusive culture and valuing diversity.

Additional desirable skills include computational modelling of protein complexes and protein-ligand complexes as well as experience with molecular biology approaches for cloning and mutagenesis of new expression constructs. An understanding of how pathogens hijack host-cell pathways will also be advantageous. The successful applicant will also have demonstrated their capacity to produce high-quality data by having first author peer-reviewed publications.
The primary focus will be on carrying out outstanding academic research which will contribute directly to collaborative papers. The project provides substantial scope for innovation, creativity and exercising scientific judgement. Fixed term: Funds are available for 12 months in the first instance.
Applications are invited for a Senior Research Associate to work with Professor Steven F. Lee in the Yusuf Hamied Department of Chemistry, University of Cambridge.
The post forms part of a translational research programme developing an imaging based drug discovery platform for neurodegenerative disease. Using quantitative single molecule imaging, the programme will characterise small protein assemblies and determine how candidate compounds alter their formation, structure and abundance. The initial focus is alpha synuclein aggregation in Parkinson's disease.
The programme will develop, miniaturise and validate a higher throughput assay, undertake compound screening and generate quantitative datasets linking compound treatment to changes in protein assembly. Working with Cambridge researchers and external academic and translational partners, the successful applicant will help develop the technology into a robust, externally deployable drug discovery platform.
The successful applicant will take substantial independent responsibility for:
Developing and validating quantitative single molecule imaging assays for protein aggregation.
Establishing reproducible workflows for higher throughput compound screening.
Performing screening experiments and developing quantitative approaches to classify and prioritise compound responses.
Building robust analysis pipelines for large imaging datasets and interpreting and presenting results.
Coordinating research across academic collaborators and external partners.
Working with commercial suppliers and technology partners to integrate compound libraries, instrumentation and assay formats.
Contributing to publications, funding applications and scientific leadership.

Postdoctoral Research Associate
Molecular and Cellular Biology of Mitochondrial Disease Models
The University of Cambridge wishes to appoint a talented postdoctoral research associate to join the research group of Prof Rita Horvath at the Department of Clinical Neurosciences and the John Van Geest Brain Repair Centre.
The position is part of a research grant from the joint call of the Action Medical Research and Action for AT, to characterise novel biomarkers of ataxia telangiectasia that support monitoring neurological progression and measuring treatment effect. The focus of your work will be to study how neuron-specific biomarkers reflect the progression of ataxia and how these change on treatment with novel antisense oligonucleotides.
You will use cutting-edge technologies, including functional studies on neuronal stem cells and human neurons. Proteomics, RNA sequencing and other omics technologies will be performed to identify the molecular mechanism of neurodegeneration and ataxia in children and adults. The over-arching aim of the research group is to develop new treatments for mitochondrial diseases and other inherited rare neuromuscular diseases using a combination of genomic, cell biology and specialized assays. You will have access to a team of experienced bioinformaticians, but have the opportunity to be trained and perform independent in-depth bioinformatic analysis of large datasets. You will have access to clinical samples from the MitoCamb neurogenetics clinic, to apply and translate novel technology and insights towards a human disease context.
We anticipate this work will lead to high-profile publications based on our track-record: Nat Comm 2026 PMID:42324264; Nat Comm 2023 PMID:36823193; Brain 2026 PMID:42634970.
The role will be located within the John Van Geest Centre for Brain Repair on the Cambridge Biomedical Campus, with state-of-the-art facilities available to group members.

The studentship will be co-supervised by Dr Jon Roozenbeek (Department of Psychology), Dr Lee de Wit (Department of Psychology) and Moira Nicolson (UK Cabinet Office)
Project description: 
Unethical decision-making is as a major societal problem. For instance, the Grenfell and Hillsborough disasters in the UK were preceded by a chain of decision failures. While there is some literature on how and why people make unethical decisions, why people tolerate or even reward those who do is understudied. This cross-cultural project will explore the psychology of unethical decision-making: what drives it, and how the public perceives it, and its connection to trust in public and private institutions.
ESRC Research Priority Areas: Security, risk and resilience, Understanding behaviour.

Understanding of survey research, randomised controlled trials, and longitudinal (cohort) studies

Knowledge of governmental accountability frameworks (especially in the UK)

Familiarity with multiple languages

You will lead computational analyses on biomarkers data, polygenic risk score calculations, and immunophenotyping data. Experience with machine learning algorithms and strong programming skills using platforms such as MATLAB, R, Bash and Python will be essential.

About us:
The post will be based at King’s College London within the QUAHRC and the NIHR Research Support Service.
The successful candidate will join a multidisciplinary team delivering an NIHR-funded methodology project focused on Collaborative Data Analysis (CDA) in applied health and social care research.
Collaborative Data Analysis brings multiple perspectives into the interpretation of research data, including those of people with lived experience. While CDA has considerable potential to improve the relevance, inclusivity and usefulness of qualitative research, existing approaches are dispersed across methodological and participatory traditions and there is limited practical guidance to help research teams implement CDA well.
The project will address this implementation gap by co-designing a national, integrated CDA implementation toolkit for applied health and social care research. The toolkit will include an implementation framework, methodological decision-support tool, training and facilitation resources, and an accessible digital platform. The project will work closely with researchers, methodological specialists, PPIE professionals and people with lived experience throughout its development.

https://www.cam.ac.uk/jobs/research-assi.description:
A position exists for a Research Assistant in the Department of Engineering, to work on mechanics of fusion materials. The post holder will be located in Central Cambridge, Cambridgeshire, UK.
We are starting a new research project focused on developing damage-tolerant materials for space and fusion-energy applications with an emphasis on refractory, body-centered cubic alloys, and high stacking fault energy alloys. Materials used in space and fusion systems must retain their structural integrity under extreme combinations of mechanical loading, temperature, and irradiation. These materials are often very brittle, but new processing techniques, including but not limited to additive manufacturing, can potentially mitigate this issue. The project will investigate the fundamental mechanisms that govern deformation and damage in these materials and use this understanding to identify new approaches to their design.
The role holder will conduct experimental research to characterise how candidate materials deform plastically (if at all) and resist fracture.
The work will involve performing mechanical characterisation including tensile, toughness and fatigue testing at room and elevated temperatures, performing electron microscopy characterisation including electron backscatter diffraction and transmission electron microscopy, and analysing/interpreting the resulting data. The candidate will be familiar with ASTM E399, E1820, and E647, dislocation mechanics, and microscopy techniques. The job will also include developing equipment including a micronotcher, vacuum-furnace and cryogenic testing system. The findings will be used to establish a first principles understanding and for the development of materials with improved resistance to damage and neutron irradiation.

https://www.cam.ac.uk/jobs/research-asso.description:
We are seeking an enthusiastic and motivated researcher to join the laboratory of Dr Suzannah Rihn at the Cambridge Institute of Therapeutic Immunology and Infectious Disease (CITIID), University of Cambridge.
Emerging and re-emerging viruses pose a continuing threat to human health. Understanding the molecular mechanisms that enable viruses to cross species barriers, adapt to new hosts and establish infections in humans is essential for improving our preparedness for future epidemics and pandemics. Our research uses a combination of molecular virology, cell biology and experimental models of virus infection to investigate the interactions between viruses and their hosts that determine the potential for viral emergence.
The successful candidate will contribute to an exciting research programme investigating the molecular determinants of viral cross-species transmission. Working as part of a collaborative research team, they will use a range of experimental approaches to investigate how viral and host factors influence infection, replication and adaptation. The project will provide opportunities to develop expertise in molecular virology, including cell culture, molecular cloning, viral reverse genetics and functional assays of virus infection.
The postholder will be expected to plan and conduct experiments, analyse and interpret data, maintain accurate research records and contribute to the preparation of scientific manuscripts and presentations. They will also participate in laboratory meetings, contribute to the wider scientific activities of the group and collaborate with colleagues within CITIID and beyond.
Applicants should have, or be close to obtaining, a PhD in biological, biochemical or biomedical sciences, with relevant experience in molecular biology or virology.
